sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.html:
Diagnosis

Tuberculosis is diagnosed through an integration of clinical assessment, microbiological confirmation, and imaging, with treatment decisions anchored to drug-susceptibility data. Classic clinical features of active pulmonary disease include a chronic cough lasting more than two to three weeks, fever, drenching night sweats, unintentional weight loss, and, in more advanced disease, hemoptysis. These features are sensitive but nonspecific, so diagnosis must be confirmed microbiologically wherever possible.

Current World Health Organization guidance positions WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostics (nucleic acid amplification tests, NAATs) as the initial test for people with signs and symptoms of TB. The cartridge-based Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assays detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA and simultaneously identify rpoB mutations conferring rifampicin resistance directly from sputum, typically within hours. {{cite:WHO_DX}} Sputum-smear microscopy for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) remains widely used but is comparatively insensitive. Mycobacterial culture on solid and liquid media remains the reference (gold) standard for definitive diagnosis and for monitoring treatment, despite turnaround times of weeks owing to the organism's slow growth. {{cite:WHO_DX}}

Chest imaging supports diagnosis: chest radiography in active pulmonary TB classically shows upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation, though appearances vary, particularly in immunocompromised or pediatric patients. Tests for TB infection—the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) and the tuberculin skin test (TST)—identify immune sensitization but cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease and cannot, on their own, confirm or exclude active TB. {{cite:WHO_DX}} Phenotypic and/or molecular drug-susceptibility testing should be pursued to guide regimen selection, especially where rifampicin or multidrug resistance is detected. {{cite:WHO_DX}}

Within a metallomic and nutritional-immunity framework, several supportive laboratory markers are commonly seen in active TB. Anemia is frequent and is predominantly an anemia of inflammation: serum iron is low while ferritin is normal or elevated and hepcidin is increased, reflecting iron sequestration into the reticuloendothelial system rather than true iron deficiency. {{cite:TB_ANEMIA}} Low serum zinc is likewise common and reflects inflammatory redistribution. {{cite:CU_ZN}} These changes are host-defense and inflammatory responses, not signals to replete iron or zinc; importantly, elevated iron status has been associated with worse outcomes in TB. {{cite:IRON_MORT}} Such metallomic markers are adjunctive and supportive only—they help characterize disease physiology and guide supportive care, but they are not diagnostic of tuberculosis itself, which still requires microbiological confirmation. {{cite:WHO_DX}}

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.html:
Frequently Asked Questions

Should iron supplements be used to treat the anemia of tuberculosis?

No—not by default. The anemia of active TB is usually an anemia of inflammation driven by hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration, characterized by low serum iron with normal or high ferritin, rather than true iron deficiency. {{cite:TB_ANEMIA}} Because iron is an essential growth factor for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, raising host iron availability can favor bacterial replication, and elevated iron status has been linked to higher mortality in TB patients. {{cite:IRON_MORT}} The mainstay is treating the infection with effective anti-TB therapy, which typically resolves the inflammatory anemia. {{cite:IRON_TB}} Iron repletion should be reserved for documented true iron-deficiency anemia and approached cautiously in active infection. {{cite:IRON_TB}}

Can diet or the microbiome affect tuberculosis?

Yes, plausibly. Host iron status and nutrition shape susceptibility and outcomes, and the gut and airway microbiomes appear to influence susceptibility to infection, progression from latent to active disease, and treatment response via the gut–lung axis. {{cite:GUT_LUNG}} {{cite:IRON_TB}} However, much of the human evidence is associative and is confounded by anti-TB antibiotics, which themselves cause prolonged gut dysbiosis, making cause and effect difficult to separate. {{cite:GUT_LUNG}} Microbiome-directed strategies remain investigational adjuncts, not established therapy. {{cite:GUT_LUNG}}

Is hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) useful for TB?

No—and on biological grounds it is the wrong lever. M. tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe: it depends on oxygen as its terminal electron acceptor and stops replicating under hypoxia, even when alternative electron acceptors are available. {{cite:AEROBE}} Hypoxia therefore restricts the organism, whereas raising tissue oxygen tension with HBOT would, in principle, relieve that restriction. Robust clinical data supporting HBOT for TB are lacking, and the underlying aerobic biology argues against it. {{cite:AEROBE}}

What is the metallomic signature of tuberculosis?

At the host–pathogen interface the immune system deploys two opposing metal strategies. It withholds iron (and manganese) from the pathogen through hepcidin-driven sequestration—"nutritional immunity"—while simultaneously flooding the macrophage phagosome with toxic concentrations of copper and zinc to poison the bacillus. {{cite:CU_ZN}} The result is a characteristic profile of systemic iron withholding alongside localized copper/zinc intoxication, which M. tuberculosis counters with dedicated metal-efflux and detoxification systems. {{cite:CU_ZN}}

Do vitamin D or NAC help in TB?

Both are rational adjuncts to—not replacements for—standard anti-TB therapy. Vitamin D induces the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin and supports antimycobacterial immunity; clinical trial results are mixed, with overall benefit on sputum conversion modest but potential signals in specific subgroups. {{cite:VITD}} N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a glutathione precursor, has antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and antimycobacterial activity in preclinical models and was safe and reduced oxidative stress in a randomized adjunctive trial; a larger trial showed it raised whole-blood glutathione and improved lung-function recovery without accelerating bacterial clearance. {{cite:NAC_RIPE}} {{cite:NAC_SEQUEL}} These agents are promising adjuncts that should be used alongside, never instead of, guideline-based treatment. {{cite:NAC_SEQUEL}}
